title: Embedding equity in implementation science: Insights from Burkina Faso and Senegal
content:
by Sarah Louart, Emmanuel Bonnet, Manuela De Allegri, Adama Faye, Kadidiatou Kadio, Oumar Mallé Samb, Valéry Ridde

Equity is a central commitment in global public health, yet it remains difficult to operationalise in low-resource settings marked by institutional fragility and strong external influences. In this essay, we argue that advancing equity within implementation science (IS) and implementation research (IR) requires locally grounded, reflexive, context-sensitive approaches that cannot be reduced to standardised technical models, such as decontextualised frameworks, universal indicators, and predefined methodological designs. Drawing on a comparative and reflexive analysis of two action-research interventions conducted more than a decade apart – a community-based indigent identification mechanism in Burkina Faso (2007–2010) and a patient navigation pilot in Senegal (2023–2025) – we illustrate the conditions under which such approaches emerge and evolve. We analyse how equity considerations were integrated into the design, implementation, and evaluation of these interventions, across four dimensions: alignment with local health priorities, mobilisation of context-sensitive and situated evidence, stakeholder involvement, and contributions to more decolonial and contextually grounded approaches. While these experiences highlight the potential of such approaches to enhance the relevance and legitimacy of interventions to improve access to healthcare, they also reveal the persistent influence of structural constraints in their operationalisation. Rather than treating equity as a purely normative aspiration, we show that its implementation involves navigating institutional fragility, policy discontinuities, unequal power dynamics, ethical dilemmas, and limited availability of actionable data. We argue that advancing equity in IS and IR requires more than technical refinement; it calls for sustained critical engagement with these constraints and a deeper transformation in how knowledge and action are co-produced in global health.
author: Sarah Louart
